section.name: Introduction
section.p: A frequent question is "How do I test my JavaScript?". There is no special API required for standard JavaScript execution—it is processed automatically. You simply fetch a page with getPage(), interact with elements using actions like click(), and inspect the resulting DOM. Tests for complex JavaScript libraries are included in the HtmlUnit repository and can be viewed here as reference examples.
When testing asynchronous code, you may need to wait briefly for AJAX responses to complete before inspecting results. Please review the AJAX FAQ entry for detailed timing guidance.

section.name: Enable and Disable JavaScript Support
section.p: JavaScript execution is enabled by default in WebClient, matching standard web browser behavior.

subsection.name: Handling JavaScript Errors
subsection.p: Key Difference: Unlike standard web browsers, HtmlUnit defaults to stopping script execution when an unhandled JavaScript error occurs. This "fail-early" default behavior is designed for automated testing environments.
You can instruct HtmlUnit to log exceptions without interrupting execution by setting throwExceptionOnScriptError to false:

subsection.name: Completely Disabling JavaScript Support
subsection.p: To optimize performance or reduce memory footprint, you can completely disable JavaScript support. The most resource-efficient method uses a specific WebClient constructor that permanently disables script capabilities:
subsection.source: WebClient webClient = new WebClient(BrowserVersion.FIREFOX, false, null, -1);

subsection.name: Temporarily Disabling JavaScript Support
subsection.p: You can toggle JavaScript execution on or off at any time using WebClientOptions. Disabling JavaScript this way prevents <script> execution and event handler invocation, though JavaScript host objects will remain instantiated in memory.

section.p: To programmatically check whether JavaScript is active, call WebClient.isJavaScriptEnabled(), which accounts for both permanent and temporary disablement states.

section.name: Prompts, Confirms, and Status Messages
section.p: Handling prompt() dialogs, confirm() dialogs, and status line updates follows the same handler pattern. See WebClient.setPromptHandler(), WebClient.setConfirmHandler(), and WebClient.setStatusHandler() for details.

section.name: Event Handlers
section.p: Standard DOM event handlers (e.g., onload, onclick, ondblclick, onmouseup, onsubmit, onreadystatechange) trigger automatically in response to user actions.

If an unhandled custom event needs to be invoked directly, you can trigger it via script execution. However, manipulating elements as an end-user would (e.g., clicking elements and changing input focus) remains the recommended approach.

section.name: Executing JavaScript in Page Context
section.p: To evaluate custom JavaScript directly within the scope of an active page or window, use HtmlPage.executeJavaScript():
section.source: final String script = "window.name;"; final String result = (String) page.executeJavaScript(script).getJavaScriptResult();
